cells.tense: You're seeing a whole thing clearly, and that's what lays the next step.
cells.act: count it out and read what the numbers show
cells.ask: Count out what a finished stretch actually produced — a season of work, a decision, a project's run. Not how it felt: what it left. Read the count and don't add to it.
cells.core:
You see a long thing all the way to its end. Once the picture goes whole in your head, you can stop holding it open and turn to whatever's next. Most people stall at the last part and keep re-reading it; you don't. That's the strength here.

So take a finished stretch and count what it left. Not how it felt, not how it looked from the outside — what the completed run actually produced. Numbers, marks, a plain list. Then read what you counted and don't read more into it. The second looking is usually the honest one, and it's what lets the next thing start from real ground.
cells.sheetLine: You finish seeing a thing, and the end is real.
cells.verb: to see a thing through to its end, whole
cells.place: at the point where a long understanding finishes and something new can start

cells.tense: Every ending out ahead is being finished in your head before anything is actually done.
cells.act: catch the first spark before you point it anywhere
cells.ask: Catch a spark before it's a project. Set down what it will be, who it's for, when it's due. Let the thing start without a plan, and don't decide what it's for.
cells.core:
You're closing things out ahead of time. An unfinished situation is landing in your body as finished — the verdict, the summary, the roll of what it cost. When a thing isn't done yet, you're resolving it anyway, so nothing arrives in you whole. You're living past the edge of it.

The finishing that's actually yours to do is smaller and closer than the one you're performing. Catch the first spark of something — a line, a minute, an idea — before you decide what it's for. Don't name it, don't line it up, don't tell anyone it's coming. Let it stay nothing yet, and hold off aiming it. One beginning allowed to stay pointless.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already closed, with your hand on the frame.
cells.act: name the form it will take, and only that
cells.ask: Name the form the next thing will take — one line, no more. How it shows up, not what it's worth. Say the line to yourself once a day, and revise nothing.
cells.core:
One version of this goes well: the long understanding closes, the thing stands finished, and you turn toward what's next without prying the old one back open. From where you stand now, the finished stretch keeps looking unfinished, so starting anything new reads as premature. Nothing closes, so nothing opens.

Direction comes back smaller than effort. Write one line: the form the next thing will take. How it shows up, not what it's worth. Plain, even clumsy — just a direction, not a question. Say it once a day and revise nothing. That line is the seed the next build grows from, and the energy arrives after it, not before.

cells.tense: You're handing finished pictures to whoever's nearby and calling it just talking.
cells.act: meet what is arriving as it arrives
cells.ask: Sit with something that recently finished — a job, a season, a relationship — and don't retell it. Not summarize: sit. Notice what's newly here, and let it land without explaining it.
cells.core:
The gift that finishes a picture and makes it plain is one you use constantly, and it's the one you'd leave out of any account of yourself. You'd say you were being helpful, stating the obvious, keeping it simple. Whole things come into view through you, for whoever's nearby, and nobody turns and says it was your doing. Neither do you.

This began closer to home than you'd describe. Before you could explain it, you noticed something clearly and said it plainly, and it landed. That early version is still in you. Take one finished thing and sit with it without retelling it — not summarize, sit — and notice what's actually different now that it's done. The picture was yours. Read it as yours for a change.
cells.sheetLine: You're the whole picture's author, and you'd say you weren't.

attempts.check: The claim I can't fully back from the record is the squad of closers I've written into Too Much — the scaffolding, the people waiting to be told the project is finished. The record gives me the capacity (Clarity, completion of seeing, sequential) and the excess (bracing at a future that can't be written in), but whether the person finishes in a group, alone, or for money is something I invented for texture. Reader's objection: 'you don't know whether my completion is a squad, a solo thing, or a habit no one sees.' The ask survives being wrong either way — noticing one thing finished cleanly in the last month and where it closed still returns the act of seeing a pattern (Calculation at work) to a person who's braced for a future finish; if the person does finish alone, the last-month frame still opens onto a real completion rather than an imagined one. The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'thirty versions of same finish' close in Too Much — it's rhythmically nice and it flatters the writer; I'll drop it and let the last-piece image carry without the riff.
